title: Derivative at a point

review.history: one secondary notation claim; broader history pending

source_policy: History distinguishes notation from concept; source inspection is recorded per claim.
purpose: Express the first-order response near a point when that local rate exists.
meaning: Compare a small output change with its input change and ask whether the ratio approaches one finite value from both sides. This describes local behavior, not the entire process or its causes.

definition.setting: A real-valued function on an open interval containing a; ordinary finite two-sided derivative.

signature.derivative: Real, if the finite two-sided limit exists

conditions: f is defined on an open interval containing a.
The quotient uses h≠0 with a+h in the domain.
The finite limit must agree from both sides.
definition.domain_notes: This card does not define one-sided endpoint derivatives, complex derivatives or generalized derivatives.

grammar.pronunciation: f prime at a is the limit as h approaches zero of the change in f divided by h.
grammar.formation_rule: Form a difference quotient for nonzero h, then bind h in a limit as h approaches zero.
grammar.precedence: f(a+h) is evaluated before subtraction; the fraction divides the entire difference by h.

parse_errors.reason: Without numerator grouping only f(a) is divided by h.
A limit is not substitution of zero into this quotient.
Absolute value at zero is a counterexample.

grammar.ast_coverage: The AST models the core right-hand expression, not the complete displayed equality. Output symbols use the explicit output binding map. Do not infer a full formula AST or arbitrary TeX parsing.

properties.conditions: All real a; nonzero h in the quotient.
properties.derivation: [(a+h)³−a³]/h=3a²+3ah+h²; the last two terms tend to zero.

properties.claim: At an interior differentiability point, Δf≈f′(a)h for small h.
properties.conditions: Differentiability at a; error depends on f and h.
properties.derivation: The definition gives f(a+h)−f(a)=f′(a)h+o(h); finite h is an approximation, not equality.

history.reader_text: One notation claim has secondary support; the concept, earlier methods, independent developments and later formalization still need research.

claims.statement: MacTutor attributes the differential symbols dx and dy and a quotient notation to a Leibniz manuscript dated 11 November 1675. This is a claim about notation in that source, not the origin of the whole concept.
claims.locator: Derivative paragraph; reference to Cajori vol. 2 p. 204
claims.uncertainty: Underlying manuscript and critical edition not inspected in this package.

research_tasks: Source earlier tangent/rate methods, independent developments, and later formalization separately.
Inspect primary/critical editions before strengthening priority assertions.

connections.reason: The derivative uses a limit of difference quotients.

connections.conditions: Appropriate hypotheses of the fundamental theorem; not every informal derivative/integral pair is interchangeable.
connections.reason: Rate and accumulation are related by a theorem under conditions.

interactive.description: Change a and signed nonzero h; compare secant slope with analytic derivative for cubic, linear and absolute-value presets. Show both sides of the corner.
invariants: For a fixed linear preset 3x+1, every valid secant slope is 3.
The absolute-value preset at a=0 has slopes of opposite sign from the two sides.
limits: The graph is finite and cannot prove limit existence.
Do not treat an extremely small floating-point h as exact zero or as exact derivative.
Display secant and analytic derivative as different outputs.
At h=0 only the finite quotient is undefined; compute/display the analytic derivative independently when it exists. Each output has its own validity state.
interactive.fallback: Table of signed h, quotient and analytic derivative; plain description of the two-sided condition.

prompts.prompt: Can a graph look smooth in a wide view and still fail to have a derivative at a point?
prompts.answer: Yes. Inspect local structure and both one-sided behaviors, and distinguish a sampled picture from a definition.

prompts.prompt: What would change if the input unit changed from seconds to minutes?
prompts.answer: The numerical rate changes with the input unit; preserve units and the same underlying phenomenon before comparing rates.
